articles.title: Alonso, sin filtro: "Perdemos tres segundos en las rectas y sí, es hasta inseguro"
articles.standfirst: Partirá 18º, pero se ve indefenso para poder luchar en la carrera. "Los rivales lo saben y dejan más espacio con nosotros"
articles.summary: Partirá 18º, pero se ve indefenso para poder luchar en la carrera. "Los rivales lo saben y dejan más espacio con nosotros"
articles.body: La lluvia del viernes le permitió subir hasta los diez mejores, pero en seco Las Vegas es un lugar en el que el Aston Martin y su motor Honda no pueden esconderse ni disimular. Fernando Alonso era muy sincero en su análisis, para una cita que está siendo un incomodo. Además señala la incongruencia de volver a EE.UU tres semanas después de estar en Austin y México, para ir la semana que viene a Qatar. Esas cosas del calendario que a los pilotos y mecánicos les incomoda sobremanera. "Ha sido exactamente como esperábamos. Monza y Las Vegas son los peores circuitos para nosotros, al tener las rectas más largas. Así que sí, perdemos unos 2,5 o 3 segundos en las rectas. En las curvas, sinceramente, fuimos bastante competitivos. Creo que estuvimos a 2,8 segundos del primer puesto en la Q1 y diría que perdimos más o menos esa diferencia en las rectas", explicaba sobre las limitaciones del motor actual de su monoplaza.. Lance Stroll lo apuntó el jueves, que la falta de potencia en rectas tan largas les compromete incluso en seguridad, por el diferencial de velocidad, y Fernando reconocía ese problema, aunque los rivales ya toman sus propias medidas. "Sí, pero creo los otros equipos son conscientes de ello", apuntaba. "Cuando van detrás de un motor Honda, necesitan dejar más espacio", añadía si filtro ni eufemismos. Las Vegas es un lugar en el que correr no es muy atractivo para el asturiano. "Siendo sincero, queda bastante lejos de Europa y es una carrera larga. Hace dos semanas estuvimos en Austin y México, a dos horas de distancia. Luego fuimos a Brasil y después a Europa y ahora volvemos aquí por 72 horas... y luego regresamos a Europa", describía. "Como también correremos en Qatar ( la próxima semana), no tiene mucho sentido celebrar esta carrera este fin de semana. Simplemente pilotar el coche... no es precisamente algo liviano. Está bien, pero obviamente no todos llevamos el mismo coche, así que no es realmente una competición ni una carrera. Para nosotros es como una exhibición", valoraba el bicampeón de F1.

articles.title: Las Vegas Grand Prix: George Russell says 'somebody has to stand up to' Max Verstappen
articles.summary: The George Russell-Max Verstappen feud surfaced again in Las Vegas, adding spice to a race where they will start on the front row.
articles.body:
The Las Vegas Grand Prix will start with two drivers on the front row who dislike each other - and after qualifying one said of the other that "somebody has got to stand up to that guy".

"That guy" is Max Verstappen, who starts his Red Bull from pole position. The driver criticising him is Mercedes' George Russell, who lines up second.

Both were promoted after the fastest qualifier, new world champion Kimi Antonelli, was demoted by a five-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allocation for the season.

Russell's beef stemmed from an incident in final practice, in which Verstappen overtook the Mercedes on the Las Vegas Strip, then veered in front of him into Turn 14.

Russell, unhappy with the Dutchman's behaviour, dived down the Red Bull's inside on braking for the corner, got alongside, and then made his displeasure known by pushing Verstappen wide, the two cars making light contact.

They were called to the stewards to discuss the incident. Verstappen was given a warning having been found to have made an "unpredictable change of direction under braking".

After qualifying, Russell told Sky Italia: "I think the warning was fine. There's nothing in the rules to say that you cannot overtake someone who is starting their lap but when you do this, you are screwing this person over.

"He does this week in, week out, with many drivers. Everybody accepts it and I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

Russell's comments were not put to Verstappen as he had finished his media commitments by the time they emerged into wider knowledge in Las Vegas.

Asked about the incident in the official news conference, Verstappen said: "Nothing happened."

When Verstappen spoke to the Dutch media, he was again reluctant to be drawn on it.

But asked whether it gave him extra motivation to beat Russell in the race, he said: "I don't need any extra motivation."

These two have history. This incident is almost exactly two years since they fell out in public following a row at the Qatar Grand Prix where Verstappen felt Russell had stepped over the line to get him a penalty that demoted him from pole position.

They exchanged insults. Russell, in remarks that echo those from Las Vegas, said: "People have been bullied by Max for years now."

Verstappen called Russell a "backstabber" and a "loser".

That was just the latest in a series of incidents - after a clash in Azerbaijan in 2022, Verstappen called Russell "Princess George" in a spat the Briton called "a little bit pathetic".

And then there was the 2025 Spanish Grand Prix. Late in the race, with Verstappen struggling with his tyres, they banged wheels as Russell attempted an overtake.

Verstappen retained the position after going off track and after being told by his team to hand the position to Russell, he moved over for the Mercedes and then appeared back on its inside and made contact with it.

He was penalised 10 seconds for that, and the following day issued a public apology for his behaviour.

All this certainly adds a hefty dose of extra spice to a race which, frankly, needs it.

This is the first of three 'dead rubbers' to close the season now both championships have been settled. There is little to fight for, and very little enthusiasm in the paddock for the final two races in the war-torn Middle East.

Despite widespread disquiet about going to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, everyone has been towing the party line on that one recently in public, that they trust governing body the FIA and Formula 1 to have made the right decision.

After qualifying, though, Verstappen came close to becoming the first to break the omerta, when he told the Dutch media "of course I would rather be at home", before repeating that he trusted the sport's bosses on the matter.

BBC Sport has been told of at least one other major driver who would rather not be going to the Middle East specifically because of concerns about safety.

As for the racing here in Sin City, it is set up beautifully.

The two drivers on the front row, as well as not troubling to hide their distaste for each other, are also the only two to have won here.

Verstappen has won two of the three events on the Strip circuit, sandwiching Russell's victory in 2024.

In theory, that could give an opportunity to McLaren's Lando Norris, who qualified fourth, and starts third as a result of Antonelli's penalty.

But the 2025 world champion was concerned about the McLaren's lack of straight-line speed.

"The pace in the car is not bad," he said. "The car is performing well, but our straight-line speed is so far off that we are not going to be able to overtake someone, so I think it's going to be a tough day."

Antonelli fastest but penalty leaves Verstappen on pole

Drivers limited to 27 laps for tyres in Qatar

His team principal Andrea Stella was more optimistic.

McLaren's battle with Red Bull for third in the constructors' championship - the two are separated by just 17 points - is one of the few major issues still to be settled this year.

Stella saw the fact that Norris had missed out on beating Russell by just 0.02secs, despite having a plastic bag caught in his floor that he said had cost 0.1secs, as reason for optimism.

As were the lessons of the Italian Grand Prix - held on a track with similarly long straights and big braking zones.

"We saw that because of this towing effect you actually can stay tangled, linked to the other cars," Stella said. "So we are definitely looking forward to tomorrow and encouraged by the fact that qualifying has been competitive.

"Because the tow effect is so big and because it's bigger than Monza, racing will be difficult to predict.

"So we need to make sure that from a driver's team point of view, we are ready for all the situations.

"It's also a circuit that may offer quite a few safety cars, and will be interesting, for instance, restarting from safety car with a tyre warm-up. Definitely an interesting one to be part of and to follow."

articles.title: Bezzecchi, pole, pero Marc Márquez saldrá por delante de Jorge Martín
articles.standfirst: El segundo lugar da más opciones de ser campeón al '93'
articles.summary: El segundo lugar da más opciones de ser campeón al '93'
articles.body: Marco Bezzecchi logró la pole de MotoGP del Gran Premio de Portugal, en Portimao. El italiano destrozó el récord de la pista para evidenciar su favoritismo. Marc Márquez supo ser explosivo para ser segundo y tendrá opciones de ser campeón, más que nada porque Jorge Martín partirá sólo séptimo y eso da más posibilidades al ilerdense. Había numerosas bajas y sustituciones: Pol Espargaró, por Maverick Viñales en el Tech3 KTM; Augusto Fernández, por Toprak Razgatlioglu en el Prima Pramac Yamaha; Iker Lecuona, por Pecco Bagnaia en el Ducati oficial y Jake Dixon, por Joan Mir, en Honda. Todos estaban pendientes del cielo, por si seguía chispeando, como hizo en el segundo libre. Las dudas sobre qué neumáticos montar y que configuración poner fueron una constante. En el inicio de la Q1, Ogura, Miller y Lecuona se atrevían a partir con gomas lisas blandas; el resto, con rayadas medias. Bastianini se esperaba un rato y acababa decidiéndose por las lisas. Pronto quedaba claro quién había elegido mejor, pues el australiano endosaba un segundo y medio al siguiente en su primer giro lanzado. Ogura lo certificaba tras una vuelta más cauta. Eso hacía que los equipos llamaran a toda prisa a los que habían partido con las gomas de agua para ponerlos la de seco. Moreira hacía un cambio casi saltando de su moto y se activaba velozmente para colocarse al frente; incluso adelantó a Ogura por el exterior en su vuelta. El japonés y el oceánico se iban a boxes a cambiar de compuestos cuando justo Lecuona también se metía en el corte. Moreira tenía un accidente bestial, volando muchos metros para darse un costalazo en el último ángulo. Milagrosamente se levantó como si nada. Hasta Marc alucinaba y se asustaba por su amigo. La Dirección de Carrera sacó la bandera roja y paró la sesión, pues había piezas en la pista. Como quedaba sólo 1:17 minutos, ya nadie tuvo tiempo de retornar y apretar, con lo que todo quedó definido. Así, pasaron Moreira y Lecuona. En la segunda parte de la parrilla estarán: 13. Miller, 14. Marini, 15. Ogura, 16. Augusto Fernández, 17. Dixon, 18. Pol Espargaró, 19. Rins, 20. Quartararo, 21. Morbidelli y 22. Bastianini. Para la Q2, ya no hubo dudas: todos partieron con neumáticos blandos y lisos. Marc partía como un rayo y se ponía al frente en su primer giro lanzado. El ‘93’ iba detrás de los del Gresini; iba tan fuerte que se echó encima de Aldeguer, aunque ni eso le impidió mejorar. Bezzecchi estaba en condiciones de batirle tras quedarse una vuelta más, pero se encontró con Di Giannantonio y tuvo que rebasarlo. Con todo, sólo le faltaron 60 milésimas para superar al mayor de los Márquez. Jorge era el más acuciado al parar a cambiar neumáticos, pues sólo era octavo. Las dos KTM y Bezzecchi optaban por variar, pero de moto y coger la segunda montura. El madrileño se activaba y forzaba detrás de ‘Diggia’, pero Fabio no le estorbó y creció. Marc mejoró en la estela de su hermano, pero ‘Bez’ voló para batir el récord y endosar casi medio segundo al del Ducati oficial. Todos se tomaron un giro de respiro para apretar en la última, pero ya ninguno pudo ser más veloz, porque sus neumáticos ya no daban para más. Así, la pole era para Bezzecchi, con Marc, segundo y Martinator, sólo séptimo. 'Bez' admitía que se sintió de maravilla. "Me encontré cómodo. Tuve que asumir algún riesgo extra, pero me salió bien", dijo en DAZN. "El objetivo era la primera línea y lo cumplimos", indicó Di Giannantonio. Marc desveló que forzó más de lo previsto. "Viendo la volada de Moreira era delicado. He cogido riesgos porque pensé que coger riesgos en Q2 me hacía minimizar riesgos en el Sprint y la carrera larga. El primer momento importante, pasado con nota. En la Sprint, el objetivo es puntuar para descartar a Bezzecchi y cerrarlo en la carrera larga", exponía.

articles.title: MotoGP to move race start time in 2027, avoid F1 clashes
articles.summary: As part of MGPSEG's plans to overhaul the weekend format, race start times will be pushed back and clashes with Formula 1 will be avoided
articles.body:
MotoGP officials have informed teams this weekend at Portimao that races will start an hour later from next season, with both the Sunday grand prix and Saturday sprint affected, Motorsport.com understands.

Under the revised schedule, the main grand prix, which has traditionally started at 2pm, will move back by an hour to 3pm. However, that start time will be subject to clashes with Formula 1, with MotoGP races potentially pushed back further to 4pm to avoid overlapping with an F1 grand prix.

Liberty Media, the company that owns both championship, does not want any F1 and MotoGP races to clash on a Sunday, and will oversee the schedules to prevent it from happening.

There will also be changes to Saturday's sprint schedule. The shorter race, first introduced in 2023, will also move back by an hour, from its traditional 3pm start to 4pm, making it a late afternoon fixture.

As Motorsport.com revealed in mid-September, MotoGP's weekend format will undergo further changes from next season, including the introduction of a new qualifying session to determine separate grids for Saturday's sprint and Sunday's grand prix.

Pedro Acosta, Red Bull KTM Factory Racing

Until now, Saturday's qualifying sessions have determined the starting grids for both races. From next season, however, the sprint grid will be set by a 15-minute qualifying session on Friday afternoon, while the grid for the longer race will be determined by the qualifying sessions held on Saturday morning.

This overhaul eliminates Friday's Practice session, which until this year has been used to establish the cut-off between riders who go directly through to Q2 and those forced to go through the second-chance session (Q1).

Under the new format, Friday's track action will feature an additional session, beginning with a 45-minute practice in the morning, followed by a second 30-minute free practice session. The day will conclude with a 15-minute qualifying session to determine the sprint grid.

On Saturday, MotoGP will reinstate the third free practice session (FP3), which will run for 20 minutes before all riders contest Q1, followed by Q2 featuring the 12 fastest competitors.

Another change will be the removal of Sunday's warm-up session, allowing riders to take part in promotional activities instead. The pitlane will also open for 10 minutes, which is not currently part of the schedule, allowing riders to complete several laps of the circuit before returning through the pitlane ahead of the race grid formation.
